tagline: A north-shore highway follows bays and channels, then takes the ferry.
intro: M-134 follows Lake Huron’s north shore through wooded country, with stretches beside bays and others inland at the bases of peninsulas. Designated in 2015, the North Huron Scenic Byway reaches from I-75 to Four Corners on Drummond Island. The Eastern Upper Peninsula Regional Planning and Development Commission identifies trails and water access as the recreational offerings recognized by the Pure Michigan Byway Program.

An earlier route east to Cedarville had carried US-2. When US-2 shifted to Mackinac Trail in 1933, the old route received other state numbers before becoming M-134. The M-134 designation arrived in 1939, replacing M-4. It then ran farther inland west of Hessel; later extensions carried it east toward DeTour. In 1989, Michigan’s transportation department added the Drummond Island segment and the ferry crossing to the route.

Driving east from I-75, cross the Pine River on Huron Shore Drive, then follow St. Martin Bay toward Hessel and Cedarville. Beyond Cedarville, the highway skirts the bays and channels separating the Les Cheneaux Islands from the mainland. At DeTour Village, the route reaches the ferry docks. Across the passage, Channel Road leads north, then east beside Sturgeon Bay before turning inland to Four Corners.

moments.title: Hessel
moments.text: Hessel’s public docks host the Antique Wooden Boat Show and Festival of the Arts each year on the second weekend of August. The community stands on M-134 north of Marquette Island, the largest of the Les Cheneaux Islands. John and Carl Hessel, both Swedish, and John A. Johnson, a Norwegian, founded it in 1885. The island group’s French name means “The Channels”: French explorers named it in the seventeenth century for the navigable passages between its islands. Those 36 islands extend along 12 miles of Lake Huron shoreline.

moments.title: DeTour Village
moments.text: DeTour Village occupies the Upper Peninsula’s eastern tip, at the shipping channel’s turn between the St. Mary’s River, Lake Huron and the Straits of Mackinac. The passage carries almost all commercial water traffic entering or leaving Lake Superior. Drummond Island’s quarries also draw vessels loading dolomite, limestone and aggregates. Storms, heavy seas and navigation losses have left freighter wrecks in and near the passage. The DeTour Reef Light continues to protect freight traffic through this waterway. M-134 continues through the village to the ferry crossing, linking this mainland shipping point with Drummond Island.

moments.title: Drummond Island
moments.text: Forest dominates Drummond Island, which also holds alvar, a rare grassy limestone plain. After the War of 1812, British troops leaving Fort Mackinac established a garrison on the island’s west end. Uncertainty over whether the island belonged to Britain or the United States limited the fortifications. Buildings bought from the North West Company on St. Joseph Island were dismantled and reassembled here to provide shelter for winter. American forces took possession in November 1828 but did not occupy the fort. A historical marker at the island’s ferry docks records Fort Drummond; surviving site features lie on private property.

practical: Drummond Island: Reaching the island on M-134 requires the Drummond Island Ferry from DeTour Village. (checked 2026-10-11)
